chapter: Guitar, John Collins and Ellington on the radio
title: Eddie Johnson and the Jazz Heritage Foundation reunion
summary: Boyhood friend Eddie Johnson, now a tenor saxophonist turned flutist, visited at Bob Singleton's house and was once scouted to replace Ben Webster.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: All right. We had a little interruption there. One thing I wanted to ask you before you go on, and that

Let's see. There was -- one of the fellow you possibly might have met over at Bob Singleton's house, a tall fellow named Eddie Johnson, and if your remember Mari Morrow Young was speaking about Eddie Johnson, as we all went to school. We all went to junior college together, you know? And Eddie was right there on the lawn, too, you know?
Over at Bob Singleton's house. That was the day that you were honored by the Jazz Heritage Foundation a few months weeks ago.

So he was just out here with his wife on a visit, and it was a beautiful weekend, you know, because we go back. I think Eddie was 13 when I first met him. Yes, as I was speaking about Eddie, but later on he was taking classical piano in The Loop, during the time when I was going through my different things with guitar and piano around the house, and then Eddie switched over to saxophone. And became a very dominant tenor saxophone player. In fact he was the one that was scouted to take Ben Webster's place with Ellington's band, before Skippy Williams. He was the man, you know? And --
Yes. Well he's very interested in flute now, because he and Jerome Richardson got together.
And he's highly interested in -- he's not in the music business as of now. He's in another profession that has lasted very well for him.
What is it that he does now?
What the heck does he do? I don't know. But it's high level work, you know?
